nodes.name: $d$-way tensor ($d$-tensor)
nodes.statement: Precisely, let $N_1$, \ldots, $N_d$ be positive integers. A $d$-dimensional array datum $T=(t_{i_1\cdots i_d})_{1\leq i_j\leq N_j, 1\leq j\leq d}$ is called a $d$-way tensor or simply a $d$-tensor of format $N_1\times \cdots\times N_d$. For a set $S$, the set of $N_1\times \cdots\times N_d$ tensors with entries in $S$ is denoted by $S^{N_1\times \cdots\times N_d}$.

nodes.name: Rank 1 tensor
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field and $V_j$ an $N_j$-dimensional vector space over $K$ with fixed basis $v_{j1}$, \ldots, $v_{jN_j}$ for $1\leq j\leq d$. Then there is a one to one correspondence between $K^{N_1\times\cdots\times N_d}$ and $V_1\otimes\cdots\otimes V_d$ by $(m_{i_1\cdots i_d})\leftrightarrow \sum_{i_1\cdots i_d}m_{i_1\cdots i_d}v_{1i_1} \otimes\cdots\otimes v_{di_d}$. A non-zero tensor corresponding to an element of $V_1\otimes \cdots\otimes V_d$ of the form $\aaa_1\otimes\cdots\otimes \aaa_d$ is called a rank 1 tensor.
differentia: corresponding to an element of $V_1\otimes \cdots\otimes V_d$ of the form $\aaa_1\otimes\cdots\otimes \aaa_d$
nodes.statement_short: A rank 1 tensor is a nonzero decomposable tensor $a_1\otimes\cdots\otimes a_d$ under the array/tensor-product correspondence.

nodes.name: Tensor rank
nodes.statement: For a general tensor $T$ of format $N_1\times\cdots\times N_d$, the rank of $T$, denoted by $\rank T$, is by definition the minimum integer $r$ such that $T$ can be expressed as a sum of $r$ rank 1 tensors, where we set the empty sum to be zero.
differentia: the minimum integer $r$ such that $T$ can be expressed as a sum of $r$ rank 1 tensors

nodes.name: Real $2\times2\times2$ tensors have two typical ranks
nodes.statement: However, there are non-empty Euclidean open subsets of $\RRR^{2\times 2\times 2}$ such that one consists of rank 2 tensors and the other one consists of rank 3 tensors. In particular, it is not possible to characterize the rank of a tensor by vanishing and/or non-vanishing of polynomials.
nodes.origin_citation: classical fact about real 2x2x2 tensors (no citation given)

nodes.name: Chevalley's Theorem (Zariski-open rank locus over $\mathbb{C}$)
nodes.statement: If the base field is $\CCC$, the set of tensors of format $p\times n\times m$ with rank at most $r$ contains a non-empty Zariski open set if and only if its Zariski closure is $\CCC^{p\times n\times m}$ (cf., Chevalley's Theorem, see e.g., \cite[p.\ 39]{har92}).
conclusions: the set of tensors of format $p\times n\times m$ with rank at most $r$ contains a non-empty Zariski open set if and only if its Zariski closure is $\CCC^{p\times n\times m}$
nodes.statement_short: Over $\mathbb{C}$, the rank-$\le r$ locus contains a Zariski-open set iff it is Zariski dense.

nodes.name: Generic rank
nodes.statement: Therefore, there exists exactly one ``typical rank of $p\times n\times m$ tensors over $\CCC$''. This is called the generic rank of $p\times n\times m$ tensors over $\CCC$ and denoted as $\grank_\CCC(p,n,m)$ or simply $\grank(p,n,m)$.

nodes.name: Generic rank equals minimal typical rank
nodes.statement: It is fairly easy to show that $\grank(p,n,m)=\min\trank(p,n,m)$ (see e.g., \cite[Chapter 6]{ssm16}).

nodes.name: Generic rank via higher secant varieties of the Segre embedding
nodes.statement: Further $r\geq \grank(p,n,m)$ if and only if the $r$-th higher secant variety of the image of Segre embedding $\PPP_\CCC\CCC^p\times\PPP_\CCC\CCC^n\times\PPP_\CCC\CCC^m \to\PPP_\CCC\CCC^{p\times n\times m}$ is the whole space $\PPP_\CCC\CCC^{p\times n\times m}$, where $\PPP_K V$ denotes the projective space consisting of one dimensional subspaces of the $K$-vector space $V$.
conclusions: the $r$-th higher secant variety of the image of Segre embedding $\PPP_\CCC\CCC^p\times\PPP_\CCC\CCC^n\times\PPP_\CCC\CCC^m \to\PPP_\CCC\CCC^{p\times n\times m}$ is the whole space $\PPP_\CCC\CCC^{p\times n\times m}$
nodes.statement_short: $r\ge$ grank iff the $r$-th secant variety of the Segre variety fills the ambient projective space.

nodes.name: Dimension-count lower bound on generic rank
nodes.statement: Thus, by counting the dimensions, we see that $\grank(p,n,m)\geq\lceil \frac{mnp}{m+n+p-2}\rceil$.

nodes.name: Threshold $p\ge(m-1)(n-1)+1$ for the dimension bound
nodes.statement: Suppose that $3\leq m\leq n\leq p$. Then $p\geq\lceil\frac{mnp}{m+n+p-2}\rceil$ if and only if $p\geq(m-1)(n-1)+1$.

nodes.name: Catalisano-Geramita-Gimigliano theorem (generic rank $=p$)
nodes.statement: Catalisano, Geramita, and Gimigliano \cite{cgg02} (see also \cite{cgg08}) proved that if $(m-1)(n-1)+1\leq p\leq mn$, then $\grank(p,n,m)=p$.

nodes.name: Tall tensor (tall array)
nodes.statement: ten Berge \cite{tb00} called a $p\times n\times m$-tensor with $(m-1)n<p<mn$ a tall array or a tall tensor

nodes.name: ten Berge's theorem on tall arrays
nodes.statement: ten Berge \cite{tb00} called a $p\times n\times m$-tensor with $(m-1)n<p<mn$ a tall array or a tall tensor and proved that $\trank(p,n,m)=\{p\}$ for these cases (see \cite[Chapter 6]{ssm16} for another proof).

nodes.name: Semi-tall tensor
nodes.statement: Here we define a $p\times n\times m$-tensor a semi-tall tensor if $(m-1)(n-1)+1\leq p\leq (m-1)n$.

nodes.name: Typical ranks of semi-tall tensors and nonsingular bilinear maps
nodes.statement: We \cite{ssm13,sms15,sms17} studied the plurality of typical ranks of semi-tall tensors and proved that if $(m-1)(n-1)+2\leq p\leq (m-1)n$, then $\trank(p,n,m)=\{p,p+1\}$ if there exists a \nonsing\ bilinear map $\RRR^m\times \RRR^n\to \RRR^{mn-p}$ and $\trank(p,n,m)=\{p\}$ otherwise, where a bilinear map $\varphi\colon V_1\times V_2\to W$ is \nonsing\ if $\varphi(x,y)=0$ implies $x=0$ or $y=0$.
nodes.origin_citation: Sumi, Sakata, Miyazaki 2013; Sumi, Miyazaki, Sakata 2015, 2017
conclusions: $\trank(p,n,m)=\{p,p+1\}$ if there exists a \nonsing\ bilinear map $\RRR^m\times \RRR^n\to \RRR^{mn-p}$
nodes.statement_short: For $(m-1)(n-1)+2\le p\le(m-1)n$, trank$=\{p,p+1\}$ iff a nonsingular bilinear map $\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^{mn-p}$ exists, else $\{p\}$.

nodes.name: Nonsingular bilinear map
nodes.statement: a bilinear map $\varphi\colon V_1\times V_2\to W$ is \nonsing\ if $\varphi(x,y)=0$ implies $x=0$ or $y=0$.

nodes.name: Former part extends to $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$
nodes.statement: We also showed in \cite{sms17} that the former part of the above mentioned result also valid in the case where $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$.
conclusions: the former part of the above mentioned result also valid

nodes.name: Slice notation $T=(T_1;\cdots;T_n)$ and $PTQ$
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field and $T=(t_{ijk})\in K^{\ell\times m\times n}$. For $1\leq k\leq n$, we set $T_k=(t_{ijk})\in K^{\ell\times m}$ and denote $T=(T_1;\cdots;T_n)$. For $P\in \glin(\ell,K)$ and $Q\in \glin(m,K)$, we set $PTQ=(PT_1Q;\cdots;PT_nQ)$.

nodes.name: Rank invariance under $T\mapsto PTQ$
nodes.statement: Note $\rank PTQ=\rank T$ by the definition of rank.

nodes.name: Typical rank
nodes.statement: \rm If the set of rank $r$ tensors over $\RRR$ of format $\ell\times m\times n$ contains a non-empty Euclidean open subset of $\RRR^{\ell\times m\times n}$, then we say $r$ is a typical rank of $\ell\times m\times n$ tensors over $\RRR$. We denote the set of typical ranks of $\ell\times m\times n$ tensors over $\RRR$ by $\trank_\RRR(\ell,m,n)$ or simply $\trank(\ell,m,n)$.
differentia: the set of rank $r$ tensors over $\RRR$ of format $\ell\times m\times n$ contains a non-empty Euclidean open subset of $\RRR^{\ell\times m\times n}$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2 (by definition of rank)
nodes.statement: By the definition of the rank, we see the following fact.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition of tensor rank.

nodes.name: Permutation invariance of typical ranks
nodes.statement: Let $n_1$, $n_2$ and $n_3$ be positive integers. Then $\trank(n_{i_1},n_{i_2},n_{i_3})=\trank(n_1,n_2,n_3)$ for any permutation $i_1$, $i_2$, $i_3$ of 1, 2, 3.

nodes.name: Flattenings $\mathrm{fl}_1$, $\mathrm{fl}_2$
nodes.statement: \rm For $T=(T_1;\cdots;T_n)\in K^{\ell\times m\times n}$, we set $$ \fl_1(T)\define(T_1,\ldots, T_n)\in K^{\ell\times mn} $$ and $$ \fl_2(T)\define \begin{pmatrix}T_1\\\vdots\\T_n\end{pmatrix}\in K^{\ell n\times m} $$ and call flattenings of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Flattenings $\mathrm{fl}_1(T)$ (slices side by side) and $\mathrm{fl}_2(T)$ (slices stacked) of a 3-tensor.

nodes.name: Flattening rank bound
nodes.statement: By the correspondence $K^{\ell\times m\times n}\leftrightarrow V_1\otimes V_2\otimes V_3$, where $V_1$ (resp.\ $V_2$, $V_3$) is a vector space over $K$ of dimension $\ell$ (resp.\ $m$, $n$) with fixed basis, flattenings correspond to natural isomorphisms $V_1\otimes V_2\otimes V_3\to V_1\otimes (V_2\otimes V_3)$ and $V_1\otimes V_2\otimes V_3\to(V_1\otimes V_3)\otimes V_2$. In particular, $\rank (\fl_1(T))\leq \rank T$ and $\rank(\fl_2(T))\leq\rank T$.
nodes.statement_short: Flattenings are tensor-space isomorphisms, so their matrix ranks bound the tensor rank from below.

nodes.name: Column/row truncation notation $M_{\le j}$, ${}_{j<}M$, $M^{\le i}$, ${}^{i<}M$
nodes.statement: \rm For $M=(\mmm_1,\ldots,\mmm_n)= \begin{pmatrix}\mmm^{(1)}\\\vdots\\\mmm^{(\ell)}\end{pmatrix} \in K^{\ell\times n}$, we set $M_{\leq j}\define(\mmm_1,\ldots, \mmm_{j})$, ${}_{j<}M\define(\mmm_{j+1},\ldots, \mmm_{n})$, $M^{\leq i}\define\begin{pmatrix}\mmm^{(1)}\\\vdots\\\mmm^{(i)}\end{pmatrix}$ and ${}^{i<}M\define\begin{pmatrix}\mmm^{(i+1)}\\\vdots\\\mmm^{(\ell)}\end{pmatrix}$.
nodes.statement_short: Notation for the first $j$ / remaining columns and first $i$ / remaining rows of a matrix $M$.

nodes.name: Determinantal ideal $I_t(M)$
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $M\in R^{\ell\times n}$. We denote by $I_t(M)$ the ideal of $R$ generated by $t$-minors of $R$.

nodes.name: Standing assumption on $m,n,p$; $u=mn-p$
nodes.statement: From now on, let $m$, $n$ and $p$ be integers with $3\leq m\leq n$ and $(m-1)(n-1)+1\leq p\leq mn$. We set $u=mn-p$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: Known results on typical ranks of tall and semi-tall tensors
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item $\grank(p,n,m)=p$. In particular, $\min\trank(p,n,m)=p$ \cite{cgg02}. \item If $p>(m-1)n$, then $\trank(p,n,m)=\{p\}$ \cite{tb00}. \item Suppose $p\leq (m-1)n$. If there exists a \nonsing\ bilinear map $\RRR^m\times\RRR^n\to\RRR^u$, then $\trank(p,n,m)=\{p,p+1\}$. Moreover, if $(m-1)(n-1)+2\leq p$, then the converse also hold true \cite{ssm13,sms15, sms17}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
nodes.origin_citation: Catalisano, Geramita, Gimigliano 2002; ten Berge 2000; Sumi, Sakata, Miyazaki 2013; Sumi, Miyazaki, Sakata 2015, 2017
assumptions: If there exists a \nonsing\ bilinear map $\RRR^m\times\RRR^n\to\RRR^u$
nodes.statement_short: grank$=p$; tall formats have the single typical rank $p$; semi-tall formats have $\{p,p+1\}$ iff a nonsingular bilinear map exists (converse for $p\ge(m-1)(n-1)+2$).

nodes.name: Typical ranks when $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$ and no nonsingular bilinear map exists
nodes.statement: Therefore, the case where $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$ and there is no \nonsing\ bilinear map $\RRR^m\times\RRR^n\to\RRR^u$ is still left open.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
nodes.statement_short: Are the typical ranks plural when $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$ and no nonsingular bilinear map $\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^u$ exists?

nodes.name: $\mathrm{trank}(p,n,m)=\mathrm{trank}(n,p,m)$
nodes.statement: Note that $\trank(p,n,m)=\trank(n,p,m)$.

nodes.name: Matrix pencil $M(\mathbf{x},A)$
nodes.statement: \rm Let $\xxx=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)$ be a row vector of indeterminates, i.e., $x_1$, \ldots, $x_m$ are independent indeterminates. For $A=(A_1;\cdots;A_m)\in\RRR^{u\times n\times m}$, we set $M(\xxx,A)\define x_1A_1+\cdots+x_mA_m\in \RRR[x_1, \ldots, x_m]^{u\times n}$.

nodes.name: $\psi(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})$ and the subspace $U(Y)$
nodes.statement: \rm Let $\aaa$ and $\bbb$ be column vectors with entries in $\RRR$ of dimension $m$ and $n$ respectively. We set $\psi(\aaa,\bbb)\define(\aaa\kprod\bbb)^{\leq p}$, where $\kprod$ denotes the Kronecker product, i.e., if $\aaa=\begin{pmatrix}a_1\\\vdots\\ a_m\end{pmatrix}$, then $\psi(\aaa,\bbb)= \begin{pmatrix}a_1\bbb\\\vdots\\ a_{m-2}\bbb\\ a_{m-1}\bbb^{\leq p-(m-2)n}\end{pmatrix}$. For $Y\in\RRR^{u\times n\times m}$, we define $U(Y)$ to be the vector subspace of $\RRR^p$ generated by $\{\psi(\aaa,\bbb)\mid M(\aaa\transpose,Y)\bbb=\zerovec\}$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
nodes.statement_short: $\psi(a,b)$ is the truncated Kronecker product $(a\otimes b)^{\le p}$; $U(Y)$ is spanned by $\psi(a,b)$ over kernel pairs $M(a^T,Y)b=0$.

nodes.name: Rank-$p$ criterion via $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))$
nodes.statement: For $T\in\msVVV$, $\rank T=p$ if and only if $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
conclusions: $\rank T=p$ if and only if $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$
nodes.statement_short: A tensor $T\in\mathscr{V}$ has rank $p$ iff $U(\mu(\sigma(T)))$ is all of $\mathbb{R}^p$.
nodes.label: lem:rank p

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement: Set $\mu(\sigma(T))=W=(W_1;\cdots;W_m)$ and $\ell=u-n$. Then by \cite[Theorem 6.5 (1)$\iff$(3)]{sms17}, we see that $\rank T=p$ if and only if there are $B=(\bbb_1, \ldots, \bbb_p)\in\RRR^{n\times p}$ and $p\times p$ diagonal matrices $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ such that $$ (\ast) \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} D_k=\diag(d_{1k},\ldots, d_{pk})&\mbox{for $1\leq k\leq m$,}\\ (d_{j1}W_1+\cdots+d_{jm}W_m)\bbb_j=\zerovec&\mbox{for $1\leq j\leq p$ and}\\ \mbox{$\begin{pmatrix} BD_1\\\vdots\\BD_{m-2}\\B^{\leq n-\ell}D_{m-1}\end{pmatrix}$ is \nonsing.} \end{array} \right. $$ First suppose that there are $B=(\bbb_1, \ldots, \bbb_p)\in\RRR^{n\times p}$ and $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ which satisfy $(\ast)$. If we set $\aaa_j=(d_{j1},\ldots, d_{jm})\transpose$ for $1\leq j\leq p$, then $$ M(\aaa_j\transpose,W)\bbb_j=\zerovec $$ for $1\leq j\leq p$ and $$ (\psi(\aaa_1,\bbb_1), \ldots,\psi(\aaa_p,\bbb_p))= \begin{pmatrix} BD_1\\\vdots\\BD_{m-2}\\B^{\leq n-\ell}D_{m-1}\end{pmatrix} $$ is \nonsing. Therefore $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$. Conversely, assume that $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$. Then there are $\aaa_1$, \ldots, $\aaa_p\in\RRR^m$ and $\bbb_1$, \ldots, $\bbb_p\in\RRR^n$ such that $\psi(\aaa_1,\bbb_1)$, \ldots, $\psi(\aaa_p,\bbb_p)$ are linearly independent. Set $\aaa_j=(d_{j1},\ldots,d_{jm})\transpose$ for $1\leq j\leq p$, $D_k=\diag(d_{1k},\ldots,d_{pk})$ for $1\leq k\leq m$ and $B=(\bbb_1,\ldots,\bbb_p)\in\RRR^{n\times p}$. Then it is easily verified that $B$ and $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ satisfy $(\ast)$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$
nodes.statement_short: Reformulate rank $p$ via [SMS17, Thm 6.5] as diagonal-matrix system $(\ast)$, then translate both directions to $\psi(a_j,b_j)$ spanning $\mathbb{R}^p$.

nodes.name: Case $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$, so $u=m+n-2$
nodes.statement: From now on, we consider the case where $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$. Then $u=m+n-2$.

nodes.name: Special tensor $A=(A_1;\cdots;A_m)$
nodes.statement: \rm We set $$ A_k\define\begin{pmatrix}O_{(k-1)\times n}\\ E_n\\ O_{(m-k-1)\times n}\end{pmatrix} \in\RRR^{u\times n} $$ for $1\leq k\leq m-1$ and $$ A_{m}\define\begin{pmatrix}O_{(m-1)\times(n-1)}&-\eee_1\\ E_{n-1}&\zerovec\end{pmatrix} \in\RRR^{u\times n}, $$ where $\eee_1=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\\vdots\\0\end{pmatrix}\in\RRR^{m-1}$ and $A=(A_1;\cdots;A_m)\in\RRR^{u\times n\times m}$.
nodes.statement_short: The special $u\times n\times m$ tensor $A$ built from shifted identity blocks and a twisted last slice.

nodes.name: Key lemma
nodes.statement: Let $y$ be an indeterminate and $a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1}\in\CCC$. Then the following conditions are equivalent, where $V_a(I)$ denotes the affine variety defined by an ideal $I$. \begin{enumerate} \item $(a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1},-1)\in V_a(I_n(M(\xxx,A)))$. \item $y^{m-1}-a_{m-1}y^{m-2}-\cdots-a_2y-a_1$ is a factor of $y^u+1$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $y$ be an indeterminate and $a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1}\in\CCC$.
nodes.statement_short: $(a_1,\dots,a_{m-1},-1)$ lies on the maximal-minor variety of $M(x,A)$ iff $y^{m-1}-a_{m-1}y^{m-2}-\cdots-a_1$ divides $y^u+1$.
nodes.label: lem:key

nodes.name: Annihilating-polynomial set $\mathscr{I}(\{\mu_t\})$
nodes.statement: \rm Let $y$ be an indeterminate and $\{\mu_t\}_{t\geq 1}$ an infinite sequence of complex numbers. We set $\msIII(\{\mu_t\}_{t\geq 1}) =\{f(y)\in\CCC[y]\mid f(y)=\sum_k c_k y^k$, $\sum_k c_k\mu_{k+t}=0$ for any $t\geq 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Polynomials whose coefficients give a linear recurrence satisfied by the sequence $\{\mu_t\}$.

nodes.name: $\mathscr{I}(\{\mu_t\})$ is an ideal
nodes.statement: It is easily verified that $\msIII(\{\mu_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ is an ideal of $\CCC[y]$.

nodes.name: Sequence $\lambda_t$ (determinants of banded matrices)
nodes.statement: Now let $a_1$, \ldots, $a_{m-1}\in\CCC$. Set $\lambda_t=0$ for $1\leq t\leq m-2$, $\lambda_{m-1}=1$ and $$ \lambda_{m-1+s}= \det\begin{pmatrix} a_{m-1}&a_{m-2}&\cdots&a_1\\ -1&\ddots&\ddots&&\ddots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&&a_1\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&&\ddots&\ddots&a_{m-2}\\ &&&&-1&a_{m-1} \end{pmatrix} $$ for $s\geq 1$, where the right hand side is an $s\times s$-determinant (some $a_i$'s may not appear for small $s$).
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda_t=0$ for $t\le m-2$, $\lambda_{m-1}=1$, and $\lambda_{m-1+s}$ is an $s\times s$ banded determinant in the $a_i$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.4 (first row expansion)
nodes.statement: By the first row expansion, we see the following
nodes.statement_short: Expand the defining determinant along its first row.

nodes.name: Linear recurrence for $\lambda_t$
nodes.statement: For $t\geq m$, we have $\lambda_t=\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{t-k}$.
nodes.label: lem:rec rel

nodes.name: $\mathscr{I}(\{\lambda_t\})$ is generated by $h(y)$
nodes.statement: By the above lemma, we see that $h(y)\in\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$. Further, since $\lambda_t=0$ for $1\leq t\leq m-2$ and $\lambda_{m-1}=1$, there is no polynomial in $\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ whose degree is less than $m-1$ except the zero polynomial, i.e., $\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ is generated by $h(y)$.
nodes.statement_short: $h$ annihilates $\{\lambda_t\}$ and no nonzero lower-degree polynomial does, so $h$ generates the ideal.

nodes.name: Matrix $N$ and maximal minors $[c_1,\ldots,c_n]_N$
nodes.statement: Set $$ N=M((a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1},-1),A) =\begin{pmatrix}a_1&&&&1\\ a_2&\ddots\\ \vdots&\ddots&\ddots\\ a_{m-1}&&\ddots&\ddots\\ -1&\ddots&&\ddots&a_1\\ &\ddots&\ddots&&a_2\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&&-1&a_{m-1} \end{pmatrix} $$ and for integers $c_1$, \ldots, $c_n$ with $1\leq c_1<\cdots<c_n\leq u$, we denote by $[c_1, \ldots, c_n]_N$ the maximal minor of $N$ consisting of the $c_1$-th, \ldots, $c_n$-th rows of $N$.
nodes.statement_short: $N=M((a_1,\dots,a_{m-1},-1),A)$ and $[c_1,\dots,c_n]_N$ its maximal minor on rows $c_1<\dots<c_n$.

nodes.name: Rank deficiency of $N$ via $\lambda_t$
nodes.statement: Under the notation above, the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item $\rank N<n$. \item $[i,m,m+1,\ldots,u]_N=0$ for $1\leq i\leq m-1$. \item $\lambda_{u+t}=0$ for $1\leq t\leq m-2$ and $\lambda_{u+m-1}=-1$. \item $\lambda_{u+t}=-\lambda_t$ for $t\geq 1$. \item $y^u+1\in\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{rank}\,N<n$ iff certain maximal minors vanish iff $\lambda_{u+t}=-\lambda_t$ iff $y^u+1$ annihilates $\{\lambda_t\}$.
nodes.label: lem:non full rank

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.5
nodes.statement: Let $$ U=\begin{pmatrix} a_{m-1}&a_{m-2}&\cdots&a_1&&1\\ -1&\ddots&\ddots&&\ddots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&&a_1\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&&\ddots&\ddots&a_{m-2}\\ &&&&-1&a_{m-1} \end{pmatrix} $$ be a $u\times u$ matrix. Then $\det({}^{t<}_{t<}U)=\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}$ for $0\leq t\leq u-1$, where $\delta_{0,t}$ is the Kronecker's delta. \ref{item:rank less than n}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:lambda u+1}: Since ${}_{m-2<}U=N$ and $\rank N<n$ by assumption, we see that $\det({}^{t<}_{t<}U)=0$ for $0\leq t\leq m-2$. Thus, we see that $\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}=0$ for $0\leq t\leq m-2$. \ref{item:lambda u+1}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:minors vanish}: We see by the first row expansions of $\det({}_{t<}^{t<}U)$ and $[t+1,m,\ldots, u]$ and the assumption that \begin{eqnarray*} 0&=&\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{u+m-1-t-k}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{k=m-t-1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{u+m-1-t-k}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{s=1}^{t+1}a_{t+2-s}\lambda_{u+1-s}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&[t+1,m,\ldots, u]_N \end{eqnarray*} for $0\leq t\leq m-2$. \ref{item:minors vanish}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:rank less than n} follows from the fact that the last $n-1$ rows of $N$ are linearly independent, \ref{item:lambda u+1}$\iff$\ref{item:rec u} follows from the facts that $\lambda_1=\cdots=\lambda_{m-2}=0$ and $\lambda_{m-1}=1$ and Lemma \ref{lem:rec rel} and \ref{item:rec u}$\iff$\ref{item:yu} follows from the definition of $\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Embed $N$ in a $u\times u$ banded matrix $U$ whose principal minors are $\lambda$'s, then chain the equivalences by row expansions and the recurrence.

nodes.name: Proof of the Key Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement: Since $(a_1,\ldots, a_{m-1},-1)\in V_a(I_n(M(\xxx,A)))$ if and only if $\rank N<n$ and $y^u+1\in\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$ if and only if $h(y)$ divides $y^u+1$, we see Lemma \ref{lem:key} by Lemma \ref{lem:non full rank}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma 4.5 with $\mathscr{I}(\{\lambda_t\})=(h)$: $y^u+1$ lies in the ideal iff $h$ divides it.

nodes.name: Degree and codimension of the maximal-minor determinantal variety
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a $u\times n$ matrix of indeterminates. Then the projective variety in $\PPP_\CCC\CCC^{u\times n}$ defined by $I_n(X)$ has degree ${u\choose n-1}$ and codimension $u-n+1$.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a $u\times n$ matrix of indeterminates.
conclusions: the projective variety in $\PPP_\CCC\CCC^{u\times n}$ defined by $I_n(X)$ has degree ${u\choose n-1}$ and codimension $u-n+1$
nodes.label: fac:deg

nodes.name: Degree count matches number of monic factors of $y^u+1$
nodes.statement: Note that ${u\choose n-1}={u\choose m-1}$ and $u-n+1=m-1$ since $u=m+n-2$. Note also that there are ${u\choose m-1}$ monic factors of $y^u+1$ of degree $m-1$ in $\CCC[y]$.

nodes.name: Linear map $\varphi_B$
nodes.statement: \rm For $B=(B_1;\cdots; B_m)\in\CCC^{u\times n\times m}$, we set $\varphi_B\colon\CCC^m\to\CCC^{u\times n}$, $(\alpha_1,\ldots, \alpha_m)\mapsto\alpha_1B_1+\cdots+\alpha_mB_m$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.8 (Key Lemma, Fact 4.6, Bezout)
nodes.statement: Then by Lemma \ref{lem:key}, Fact \ref{fac:deg} and Bezout's theorem, we see the following
nodes.statement_short: Count intersection points via the Key Lemma against the Bezout bound from the determinantal degree.

nodes.name: Transverse intersection at $\binom{u}{m-1}$ points
nodes.statement: Let $\PPP_\CCC(\image\varphi_A)$ be the linear subspace of $\PPP_\CCC\CCC^{u\times n}$ defined by $\image\varphi_A$. Then $\PPP_\CCC(\image\varphi_A)$ and $V_p(I_n(X))$ intersect transversely at ${u\choose m-1}$ distinct points, where $V_p(I)$ denotes the projective variety defined by the homogeneous ideal $I$.
assumptions: Let $\PPP_\CCC(\image\varphi_A)$ be the linear subspace of $\PPP_\CCC\CCC^{u\times n}$ defined by $\image\varphi_A$.
conclusions: Then $\PPP_\CCC(\image\varphi_A)$ and $V_p(I_n(X))$ intersect transversely at ${u\choose m-1}$ distinct points

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.9 (implicit function theorem)
nodes.statement: By the implicit function theorem, we see the following fact.
nodes.statement_short: Transversality persists under small perturbation by the implicit function theorem.

nodes.name: Stable count of real points near $A$
nodes.statement: There is a Euclidean open neighborhood $\msUUU$ of $A$ in $\RRR^{u\times n\times m}$ such that if $B\in\msUUU$, then $\varphi_B$ is injective and the number of real points of $V_p(I_n(M(\xxx,B)))\subset\PPP_\CCC\CCC^m$ is the number of real monic polynomials of degree $m-1$ which divide $y^u+1$, where we say a point of a complex projective space is real if all possible ratios of its homogeneous coordintes are real numbers.
conclusions: There is a Euclidean open neighborhood $\msUUU$ of $A$ in $\RRR^{u\times n\times m}$
the number of real points of $V_p(I_n(M(\xxx,B)))\subset\PPP_\CCC\CCC^m$ is the number of real monic polynomials of degree $m-1$ which divide $y^u+1$
nodes.statement_short: Near $A$, $\varphi_B$ is injective and the real points of the determinantal locus correspond to real monic degree-$(m-1)$ divisors of $y^u+1$.

nodes.name: $\alpha(m,n)$: number of real monic divisors of $y^u+1$
nodes.statement: We denote the number of real monic polynomials of degree $m-1$ which divides $y^u+1$ by $\alpha(m,n)$.
nodes.genus: the number of real monic polynomials of degree $m-1$

nodes.name: Formula for $\alpha(m,n)$
nodes.statement: $$ \alpha(m,n)= \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} {u/2\choose (m-1)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ and $n$ are odd,}\\ {(u-1)/2\choose (m-2)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ is even and $n$ is odd,}\\ {(u-1)/2\choose (m-1)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ is odd and $n$ is even and}\\ 0&\quad\mbox{if $m$ and $n$ are even.} \end{array} \right. $$
assumptions: From now on, we consider the case where $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$.
conclusions: \alpha(m,n)= \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} {u/2\choose (m-1)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ and $n$ are odd,}\\ {(u-1)/2\choose (m-2)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ is even and $n$ is odd,}\\ {(u-1)/2\choose (m-1)/2}&\quad\mbox{if $m$ is odd and $n$ is even and}\\ 0&\quad\mbox{if $m$ and $n$ are even.} \end{array} \right.
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha(m,n)$ is a binomial coefficient depending on the parities of $m,n$, and is $0$ when both are even.
nodes.label: lem:alpha m n

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.11 (shrinking $\mathscr{U}$)
nodes.statement: By replacing $\msUUU$ to a smaller neighborhood if necessary, we may assume that $\rank (M(\aaa,B)_{\leq n-1})=n-1$ for any $B\in\msUUU$ and $\aaa\in\RRR^m\setminus\{\zerovec\}$ (cf.\ \cite[Corollary 4.20]{sms17}). Then we have the following fact.
nodes.statement_short: Shrink $\mathscr{U}$ so the first $n-1$ columns of $M(a,B)$ keep full rank; then each real point gives a unique $[\psi(a,b)]$.

nodes.name: Number of generators $[\psi(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})]$ equals $\alpha(m,n)$
nodes.statement: Suppose $B\in\msUUU$. Then $\#\{[\psi(\aaa,\bbb)]\in\PPP_\RRR\RRR^p\mid M(\aaa,B)\bbb=\zerovec, \aaa\in\RRR^m\setminus\{\zerovec\}, \bbb\in\RRR^n\setminus\{\zerovec\}\} =\alpha(m,n)$, where $[\xxx]$ denotes the point of $\PPP_\RRR\RRR^p$ defined by $\xxx\in\RRR^p\setminus\{\zerovec\}$.
nodes.label: lem:number gen

nodes.name: Plural typical ranks when $m-1$, $n-1$ are not bit-disjoint
nodes.statement: If $m-1$ and $n-1$ are not bit-disjoint, then $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$, where two positive integers are bit-disjoint if there are no 1's in the same place of their binary notation.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.label: fact:bit dis

nodes.name: Bit-disjoint integers
nodes.statement: two positive integers are bit-disjoint if there are no 1's in the same place of their binary notation.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
differentia: there are no 1's in the same place of their binary notation

nodes.name: Known cases with $\mathrm{trank}=\{p,p+1\}$
nodes.statement: \rm $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$ in the following cases. \begin{enumerate} \item Both $m$ and $n$ are even. \item $m=5$ and $n\equiv 5,6,7,8\pmod 8$. \item $m=6$ and $n\equiv 2,4,5,6,7,8\pmod 8$. \item $m=7$ and $n\equiv 3,4,5,6,7,8\pmod 8$. \item $m=8$ and $n\equiv 2,3,4,5,6,7,8\pmod 8$. \item $m=9$ and $n\equiv 9,10,11,12,13,14,15,16\pmod {16}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.label: ex:known

nodes.name: Tensors $A''$, $A'$, $W_0$, map $\rho$ and neighborhood $\mathcal{U}$
nodes.statement: Set $ A''=(A_2;\cdots;A_{m-2};A_m;-A_{m-1};-A_{1})$. Then there is a permutation matrix $P\in\glin(u,\RRR)$ such that ${}_{p<}\fl_1(PA'')=-E_u$. Set $A'=PA''$ and $W_0=\fl_1(A')_{\leq p}$. Further set $\rho\colon\RRR^{u\times n\times m}\to\RRR^{u\times n\times m}$, $B=(B_1;\cdots;B_m)\mapsto P(B_2;\cdots;B_{m-2};B_m;-B_{m-1};-B_{1})$ and $\UUUUU=\mu^{-1}(\rho(\msUUU))$, where $\mu$ is the map defined in Definition \ref{def:sigma nu}.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: Permute and sign-change the slices of $A$ so its tail flattening is $-E_u$; pull $\mathscr{U}$ back to an open set $\mathcal{U}=\mu^{-1}(\rho(\mathscr{U}))$ of $W$'s.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{U}$ is an open neighborhood of $W_0$
nodes.statement: Then $\UUUUU$ is an open neighborhood of $W_0$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.3 (by Lemma 4.11)
nodes.statement: Further, we see the following fact by Lemma \ref{lem:number gen}.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: Transport Lemma 4.11 through the change of coordinates $\rho$ and $\mu$.

nodes.name: Generator count for $T\in\sigma^{-1}(\mathcal{U})$
nodes.statement: If $T\in\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$, then $\#\{[\psi(\aaa,\bbb)]\in\PPP_\RRR\RRR^p\mid M(\aaa,\mu(\sigma(T)))\bbb=\zerovec, \aaa\in\RRR^m\setminus\{\zerovec\}, \bbb\in\RRR^n\setminus\{\zerovec\}\} =\alpha(m,n)$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement: Since $\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$ contains $\tau(W_0)$, $\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$ is not an empty set. Therefore, we see by Lemma \ref{lem:rank p} that if $\alpha(m,n)<p$, then there exists a non-empty Euclidean open subset $\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$ of $\RRR^{n\times p\times m}$ consisting of tensors of rank larger than $p$. Further, since we see by \cite[Theorem 8.1]{sms17} that typical ranks of $n\times p\times m$ tensors are less than or equal to $p+1$, we see the following fact.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: If $\alpha<p$ then $U$ cannot span $\mathbb{R}^p$ on the nonempty open set $\sigma^{-1}(\mathcal{U})$, so rank exceeds $p$ there; typical ranks are at most $p+1$.

nodes.name: $\alpha(m,n)<p$ implies plural typical ranks
nodes.statement: If $\alpha(m,n)<p$, then $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.label: lem:less than p

nodes.name: Main theorem: plural typical ranks for $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$
nodes.statement: Suppose $3\leq m\leq n$ and $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$. Then $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$ in the following cases. \begin{enumerate} \item $m=3$ or $m=4$. \item $m=5$ and $n\leq 26$ or $n=28$. \item $m=6$ and $n\leq 34$. \item $m=7$ and $n\leq 16$. \item $m=8$ and $n\leq 16$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: For $p=(m-1)(n-1)+1$, $\mathrm{trank}(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$ for $m\in\{3,4\}$ and listed ranges of $n$ for $m=5,\dots,8$.
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.5
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:alpha m n} and computation, we see that $\alpha(m,n)<p$ in the following cases: (1) $m=3$ or $m=4$, (2) $m=5$ and $n\leq 26$ or $n=28$, (3) $m=6$ and $n\leq 34$, (4) $m=7$ and $n\leq 12$, (5) $m=8$ and $n\leq 14$ and (6) $m=9$ and $n=10$. Thus, we see the result by Example \ref{ex:known} and Lemma \ref{lem:less than p}.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\alpha(m,n)<p$ from Lemma 4.10 in the listed ranges and combine with Example 5.2 and Lemma 5.4.

nodes.name: Converse of the bit-disjointness criterion fails
nodes.statement: \rm Set $m=3$ and $n=5$. Then $m-1$ and $n-1$ are bit-disjoint. However, by Theorem \ref{thm:main}, we see that $\trank(n,p,m)=\{p,p+1\}$. Thus the converse of Fact \ref{fact:bit dis} does not valid.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
nodes.statement_short: $m=3,n=5$ are bit-disjoint yet have plural typical ranks, so Fact 5.1's converse fails.

nodes.name: Reformulate rank $p$ via [SMS17, Thm 6.5]
nodes.statement: Set $\mu(\sigma(T))=W=(W_1;\cdots;W_m)$ and $\ell=u-n$. Then by \cite[Theorem 6.5 (1)$\iff$(3)]{sms17}, we see that $\rank T=p$ if and only if there are $B=(\bbb_1, \ldots, \bbb_p)\in\RRR^{n\times p}$ and $p\times p$ diagonal matrices $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ such that $$ (\ast) \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} D_k=\diag(d_{1k},\ldots, d_{pk})&\mbox{for $1\leq k\leq m$,}\\ (d_{j1}W_1+\cdots+d_{jm}W_m)\bbb_j=\zerovec&\mbox{for $1\leq j\leq p$ and}\\ \mbox{$\begin{pmatrix} BD_1\\\vdots\\BD_{m-2}\\B^{\leq n-\ell}D_{m-1}\end{pmatrix}$ is \nonsing.} \end{array} \right. $$
nodes.statement_short: Set $W=\mu(\sigma(T))$ and invoke the cited criterion: rank $p$ iff system $(\ast)$ is solvable.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: ($\ast$) solvable implies $\dim U=p$
nodes.statement: First suppose that there are $B=(\bbb_1, \ldots, \bbb_p)\in\RRR^{n\times p}$ and $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ which satisfy $(\ast)$. If we set $\aaa_j=(d_{j1},\ldots, d_{jm})\transpose$ for $1\leq j\leq p$, then $$ M(\aaa_j\transpose,W)\bbb_j=\zerovec $$ for $1\leq j\leq p$ and $$ (\psi(\aaa_1,\bbb_1), \ldots,\psi(\aaa_p,\bbb_p))= \begin{pmatrix} BD_1\\\vdots\\BD_{m-2}\\B^{\leq n-\ell}D_{m-1}\end{pmatrix} $$ is \nonsing. Therefore $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$.
nodes.statement_short: Read off $a_j$ from the diagonals; the $\psi(a_j,b_j)$ form a nonsingular matrix, so $\dim U=p$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: Converse: extract independent $\psi(a_j,b_j)$
nodes.statement: Conversely, assume that $\dim U(\mu(\sigma(T)))=p$. Then there are $\aaa_1$, \ldots, $\aaa_p\in\RRR^m$ and $\bbb_1$, \ldots, $\bbb_p\in\RRR^n$ such that $\psi(\aaa_1,\bbb_1)$, \ldots, $\psi(\aaa_p,\bbb_p)$ are linearly independent.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $\dim U=p$ and pick $p$ independent generators $\psi(a_j,b_j)$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: Build $B$, $D_k$ satisfying ($\ast$)
nodes.statement: Set $\aaa_j=(d_{j1},\ldots,d_{jm})\transpose$ for $1\leq j\leq p$, $D_k=\diag(d_{1k},\ldots,d_{pk})$ for $1\leq k\leq m$ and $B=(\bbb_1,\ldots,\bbb_p)\in\RRR^{n\times p}$. Then it is easily verified that $B$ and $D_1$, \ldots, $D_m$ satisfy $(\ast)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $D_k$ and $B$ from the $a_j,b_j$; they satisfy $(\ast)$.
nodes.section: 3 A condition of an $n\times p\times m$-tensor to be of rank $p$

nodes.name: Auxiliary banded matrix $U$
nodes.statement: Let $$ U=\begin{pmatrix} a_{m-1}&a_{m-2}&\cdots&a_1&&1\\ -1&\ddots&\ddots&&\ddots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&&a_1\\ &&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&&\ddots&\ddots&a_{m-2}\\ &&&&-1&a_{m-1} \end{pmatrix} $$ be a $u\times u$ matrix. Then $\det({}^{t<}_{t<}U)=\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}$ for $0\leq t\leq u-1$, where $\delta_{0,t}$ is the Kronecker's delta.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the $u\times u$ banded matrix $U$ whose trailing principal minors are $\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}$.

nodes.name: (1) implies (3)
nodes.statement: \ref{item:rank less than n}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:lambda u+1}: Since ${}_{m-2<}U=N$ and $\rank N<n$ by assumption, we see that $\det({}^{t<}_{t<}U)=0$ for $0\leq t\leq m-2$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $N$ is a submatrix of $U$, rank deficiency kills the relevant minors, giving the $\lambda$ conditions.

nodes.name: (3) implies (2)
nodes.statement: \ref{item:lambda u+1}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:minors vanish}: We see by the first row expansions of $\det({}_{t<}^{t<}U)$ and $[t+1,m,\ldots, u]$ and the assumption that \begin{eqnarray*} 0&=&\lambda_{u+m-1-t}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{u+m-1-t-k}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{k=m-t-1}^{m-1}a_{m-k}\lambda_{u+m-1-t-k}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&\sum_{s=1}^{t+1}a_{t+2-s}\lambda_{u+1-s}+\delta_{0,t}\\ &=&[t+1,m,\ldots, u]_N \end{eqnarray*} for $0\leq t\leq m-2$.
nodes.statement_short: First-row expansions identify the vanishing $\lambda$ expressions with the maximal minors of $N$.

nodes.name: Remaining implications
nodes.statement: \ref{item:minors vanish}$\Longrightarrow$\ref{item:rank less than n} follows from the fact that the last $n-1$ rows of $N$ are linearly independent, \ref{item:lambda u+1}$\iff$\ref{item:rec u} follows from the facts that $\lambda_1=\cdots=\lambda_{m-2}=0$ and $\lambda_{m-1}=1$ and Lemma \ref{lem:rec rel} and \ref{item:rec u}$\iff$\ref{item:yu} follows from the definition of $\msIII(\{\lambda_t\}_{t\geq 1})$.
nodes.statement_short: (2)⇒(1) by independence of the last rows; (3)⇔(4) by the recurrence; (4)⇔(5) by definition of $\mathscr{I}$.

nodes.name: $\sigma^{-1}(\mathcal{U})$ is nonempty
nodes.statement: Since $\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$ contains $\tau(W_0)$, $\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$ is not an empty set.
nodes.statement_short: $\tau(W_0)\in\sigma^{-1}(\mathcal{U})$, so this open set is nonempty.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement: Therefore, we see by Lemma \ref{lem:rank p} that if $\alpha(m,n)<p$, then there exists a non-empty Euclidean open subset $\sigma^{-1}(\UUUUU)$ of $\RRR^{n\times p\times m}$ consisting of tensors of rank larger than $p$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 3.6 and the generator count, $\alpha<p$ forces rank $>p$ on an open set.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors

nodes.name: Upper bound $p+1$ and conclusion
nodes.statement: Further, since we see by \cite[Theorem 8.1]{sms17} that typical ranks of $n\times p\times m$ tensors are less than or equal to $p+1$, we see the following fact.
nodes.statement_short: Typical ranks are at most $p+1$ by [SMS17, Thm 8.1], giving $\{p,p+1\}$.
nodes.section: 5 Plural typical ranks of some formats of 3-tensors
